summary: For ages 9–11: pupils learn to plan scientific enquiries by choosing the right enquiry type for a question and, within a fair test, assigning each factor as the variable to change (independent), measure (dependent), or keep the same (control), and justifying why control makes a result valid. The central active experience is designing a plan and seeing how an uncontrolled variable makes a result impossible to interpret. Supporting activities assess variable roles and enquiry-type matching and probe pupils' justifications. Alternatives include categorisation-and-matching questions and a Socratic plan-interrogation; a labelled reference image is a scaffold only.
misconceptions: Defaulting to a fair test for every question, including ones better answered by observing over time, pattern-seeking, classifying or research (the AKSIS over-default persists into upper KS2).
Listing controlled variables without understanding why control is necessary — not connecting uncontrolled variables to invalid, uninterpretable results.
Confusing the independent (changed) and dependent (measured) variables, or thinking the thing you measure is something you set.
Believing 'more variables changed = a better/bigger experiment', missing that changing more than one destroys attribution.
Thinking planning is a formality to rush past, rather than the step that determines whether the results can answer the question at all.

activities.title: Design the plan, then run it: make a confound wreck your experiment
steps: Take a real question (e.g. 'Do plants grow taller with more sunlight?') and plan an investigation before doing anything.
Choose one enquiry type from the five: fair/comparative test, observing over time, pattern-seeking, classifying/identifying, or research.
Sort each factor into 'change' (the one input you vary), 'measure' (the output/result), and 'keep the same' (controls).

Run the plan. If you left factors uncontrolled — e.g. the sunny plant also got more water and a bigger pot — observe how the result comes back ambiguous: 'light, water and pot size all differed, so we can't say which caused the growth.'
Fix the plan by keeping every other factor you can the same so only one is changed, re-run, and compare how a cleaner plan gives an answer you can more fairly put down to that one change.
Notice that changing several factors at once does not make a 'bigger or better' experiment — it only destroys your ability to attribute the effect to any one cause.

Try a question that is NOT best answered by a fair test (e.g. 'How does the Moon's appearance (its phase) change over a month?') and see that choosing 'fair test' misfires — observing over time fits better.
activities.insight: Controlling variables is not a rote rule: it removes rival explanations so a difference in results can be attributed to the one thing you changed. Changing more than one factor does not make the experiment stronger — it makes the cause unknowable. Different questions need different enquiry types, so a fair test is not always the right tool.

activities.title: Sort the variables and match the enquiry type
steps: Categorise a list of factors in a given investigation into independent (change), dependent (measure), and control (keep the same) roles.
Match several questions to their best-fitting enquiry type among the five named types.
Answer 'why must we keep X the same?' by naming the rival explanation it rules out.
activities.insight: Pupils can distinguish the thing you set from the thing you measure, and can pick an enquiry type fit to the question — the knowledge that underpins independent planning.

activities.title: Interrogate the plan: what else might be affecting your result?
steps: Present a draft investigation plan to a 'scientist' partner or mentor.
Respond to probing questions such as 'What else might be affecting your result?' and 'Which rival explanation does each control rule out?'
Revise the plan to remove hidden uncontrolled variables and to confirm the enquiry type fits the question.
activities.insight: Articulating and defending a plan can surface hidden confounds and push the 'why control?' reasoning to become explicit.

checkQuestion: A student wants to know if plants grow taller with more sunlight. They put one plant on a sunny windowsill and another in a dark cupboard — but they also water the sunny one more and use a bigger pot for it. After two weeks the sunny plant is taller. Can they be sure it was the sunlight? Talk me through what's wrong with the test, what needs to be kept the same, and why that matters for trusting the answer.
checkAnswer: No — more than one thing differs (light, water, pot size), so you can't tell which caused the taller plant; the test is confounded. A strong response says you must keep water, pot size, soil, plant type and starting height the same, changing ONLY the light, so that any difference in growth can be attributed to light alone. It frames controlling variables as what makes the result VALID — it removes rival explanations — and may name this as a fair/comparative enquiry rather than, say, observation over time.
